title: Christie Blatchford: Police shooting victim's family 'disgusted' by officer's lack of remorse at inquest
subtitle: Jermaine Carby's relatives were crushed that Const. Ryan Reid, said he 'wouldn't change anything,' and appeared to reserve his greatest empathy for himself
article: For the first time in almost 20 months, relatives of Jermaine Carby have learned the name and seen the face of the Peel Regional Police officer who shot and killed their 33-year-old son and cousin.
It was, they said afterward, an altogether underwhelming experience.
They were crushed that the officer, Const. Ryan Reid, said he "wouldn't change anything" about that night and disappointed he expressed no regret.
In fact, Reid appeared to reserve his greatest empathy for himself.

At one point, he told coroner's counsel Michael Blain, "This is something that I will live with for the rest of my life ... I'm a young man and now I have to live with this for the rest of my life. I've relived this incident ... I wouldn't change anything, I just wish Mr. Carby had dropped the knife."
Reid was cleared of wrongdoing by the province's Special Investigations Unit in July 2015, which found he was acting in lawful self-defence after Carby brandished a knife at him.

But because of concerns about the way police managed the knife at the scene - contrary to SIU protocols, it was collected by a Peel officer and given to an acting sergeant, apparently before the SIU arrived, and only hours later handed over - SIU director Tony Loparco was sharply critical of police conduct.
The removal of the knife "cast a pall over the integrity of the SIU's investigation," Loparco said at the time.

And though he said he was satisfied that the totality of the evidence established Carby had been wielding the knife, its curious removal "ensures that some members of the community will harbour concerns" over whether it existed.
Some of those community members, from the group Black Lives Matters, sat front-row centre Friday with Carby's mother, Lorna Robinson, and his cousin, La Tanya Grant.

Grant, the articulate family spokesperson, told reporters outside court they were "disgusted by what happened today. Clearly, there's lies in the courtroom ... there was no knife present and the knife was planted."
Robinson was clearly wounded by the lack of remorse she saw in Reid, though she said seeing and hearing him gave her "a release, at least."

Grant was also furious that after his testimony, Reid, like other Peel officers who have testified here, was spirited away by security, and left the courthouse in a black SUV with heavily tinted windows.

While photographs can't be taken on courthouse property, it's the norm that once witnesses step outside, reporters can and do take their pictures: it's an integral part of what's supposed to be a public process.

Perhaps in anticipation of that disappearing act, someone in the public gallery apparently took a picture of Reid while he was testifying and posted it on a social media site. Coroner Dr. Bill Lucas later said he was "very concerned about this" and said Reid should be "able to testify knowing he will not be harassed during the process."
As for the substance both of Carby's circumstances and of Reid's testimony, it was jarringly familiar.

The 33-year-old Carby had a well-documented history of mental instability - he'd been hospitalized four times during the six months before his death, his most recent release coming just 12 days earlier - that involved violence fundamentally directed at himself.
The jury has heard he was often depressed and suicidal.

Blain said in his opening statement this week that Carby had tried to kill himself by using drugs cut with gas and bleach, made an attempt to cut his own throat, considered jumping in front of a subway or into traffic, once grabbed a syringe and threatened to inject air into his veins and recently had tried to disarm a police officer.
The bare bones of that history came up on the police computer when Const. Jason Senechal, the officer who originally stopped the car in which Carby was but a passenger, ran his name.
Senechal, who testified earlier, admitted he'd been "carding" Carby, doing a street check for no investigative reason but to create a record for the force's information system.
Carby was with Acacio Barros, who was driving his sister's car.
Former school friends, the two had recently re-connected after Reid's return from Vancouver, where, Barros said, he went after he came out of the closet as a gay man.

Earlier that night, they had smoked methamphetamine, and were on their way to find some food when Senechal spotted a slightly crooked rear licence plate on the car, and noticed the front headlights weren't on.
Senechal asked Barros for his driver's licence, showed him the askew plate and the dark front lights, and had him take a roadside breathalyzer, which he passed.
Then Senechal turned his attention to Carby, in the passenger seat.
According to Barros, Carby was "really offended" when Senechal, accompanied by Reid, who by now had arrived at the scene, asked him to get out of the car.
In short order, Carby got angrier and, Barros told the SIU, pulled a knife.

Senechal and Reid and Jason Valquez, another officer, all pulled their guns and began backing away from Carby, shouting the usual commands to drop the knife, with Carby reportedly shouting, "Shoot me! Shoot me!"
Barros' audio-recorded statement to the SIU was played this week; police haven't been able to locate him yet, so it may be all the jurors will hear from him.
Four minutes after Reid arrived, he fired his 40-calibre Smith and Wesson seven times. Three bullets hit Carby, one in the chest, one in the arm and one in the centre of his back.
Reid told Faisal Mirza, one of the lawyers for the family, that "I did not shoot Mr. Carby in the back intentionally," but rather that he must have been turning around at the time he fired.
"Fair to say you can't hit someone squarely in the back unless his back is to you?" Mirza asked. "Yes," Reid replied.
The inquest resumes Monday.
